names.name: the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned (ajāta, abhūta, akata, asaṅkhata)
the element of nibbāna with and without residue (saupādisesā / anupādisesā nibbānadhātu)
the further shore, the island, the refuge, the peaceful, the sublime (SN 43 synonyms)

descriptions: the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion (SN 38.1)
the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation (MN 26; AN 3.32)
the highest happiness (Dhp 203–204); the deathless state (Dhp 21)
the unshakeable liberation of mind — 'unshakeable is my release; this is the last birth' (SN 56.11)
negations: there is that sphere where there is no earth, water, fire or air, no sphere of infinite space … no neither-perception-nor-non-perception, neither this world nor another, neither sun nor moon; no coming, going, staying, passing away or arising; without support, without occurrence, without object — this is the end of suffering (Ud 8.1)
there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned; were there not, no escape from the born, become, made, conditioned would be known (Ud 8.3)
consciousness that does not manifest (viññāṇaṃ anidassanaṃ), infinite, radiant all round, where earth, water, fire and air find no footing (DN 11; MN 49)
the Tathāgata released from reckoning by form … is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom like the ocean; 'is reborn', 'is not reborn', 'both', 'neither' do not apply (MN 72)
relation_to_self: Not a self and not the self's true nature: all conditioned things are impermanent and suffering, and 'all phenomena (sabbe dhammā) are not-self' (Dhp 277–279; AN 3.136). The ordinary person 'conceives nibbāna as mine, delights in nibbāna', the Tathāgata does not (MN 1).
relation_to_world: Not a cause, ground or source of the world: the world (loka), its origin, its cessation and the way to its cessation are declared 'in this fathom-long body with its perception and mind' (SN 2.26; AN 4.45). Nibbāna is the cessation of the world of the six senses, not what the world is made of.
caveat: The suttas speak of one unconditioned element (asaṅkhatā dhātu), but deny that it is a self, a creator, a Brahman or a metaphysical ground from which beings or the world proceed: the Brahmajāla (DN 1) lists the views that identify a permanent self or world as views born of contact and craving, and MN 1 criticises 'conceiving' even nibbāna. Any reading of nibbāna as 'the one reality called by many names' is an interpretation the tradition itself would reject if it implies a substantial essence; it accepts only that the same unconditioned is named by many epithets (SN 43).

names.name: paramattha-dhamma nibbāna (the fourth ultimate reality, beside citta, cetasika and rūpa)

descriptions: the one unconditioned dhamma, outside the five aggregates and the three periods of time; object of the path and fruition consciousness
one in nature (santi-lakkhaṇa, the characteristic of peace) but described as with residue (sa-upādisesa, the arahant's living) and without residue (anupādisesa, at the arahant's death) (Iti 44)
described by the commentaries as existing (atthi) and not mere non-existence, against those who say it is only the absence of the defilements
negations: not a self (sabbe dhammā anattā — Dhp 279, read by the commentaries to include nibbāna)
not produced by the path but realised by it; without arising, change or passing away (AN 3.47)
relation_to_self: Nibbāna is anattā; there is no self that attains it — 'suffering exists, but no sufferer; nibbāna exists, but no one who is extinguished' (Visuddhimagga 16.90, a commentarial verse; see U37).
relation_to_world: The unconditioned is distinct from the conditioned world (saṅkhata) and is not its cause; the world is dependently arisen.
caveat: Theravāda affirms nibbāna as a real, single unconditioned dhamma but explicitly rejects that it is a self, a soul-substance, a creator or a cosmic ground; it would reject the identification of nibbāna with Brahman or ātman made in some reconciliations (the Kathāvatthu and the commentaries argue against any permanent self).
notes: The commentarial and Abhidhamma details are skeleton pointers; U37 owns the Abhidhamma and Visuddhimagga.
